title: Fan-out on Write

post.author: u/whisperwall_nerys
post.title: I moderate a city gossip app at night. At 23:01, thousands of people were reading congratulations on an engagement that, on their screens, nobody had announced.

blocks.text: I'm the night moderator at Whisperwall, the gossip app everyone in Stellmarsh pretends not to use. I clear reports, hide the cruel stuff, and sort the tip inbox for Yolanda Fitzroy, who writes the Overheard column from it. Every account has a timeline: the posts of the accounts it follows, newest first. Kayode, our developer, once explained how they're built. A new post goes on the fan-out queue, and the fan-out workers copy it into the stored timeline of each of the poster's followers, one after another down the follower list. Opening the app is then one quick read. We run seven workers, and each copies 100 timelines a second.
Seven hundred a second had always looked like plenty.

At 23:00 on Friday, Oriane Merrivane posted. She hosts the breakfast show, and 1,890,000 accounts follow her. The post was one word, *Engaged*, and a photo of a ring. Her friends answered within two minutes: Bex at 23:00:14, Tavish at 23:00:31, Sabeth at 23:00:52, Noemi at 23:01:40. Each has fewer than 250 followers.

By 23:02 Yolanda's inbox was filling with screenshots. Timelines with SHE SAID YES, and about time!!, and Congratulations, both of you, and nothing above them. Who said yes? People asked whether Oriane had posted something and deleted it. I checked. Nothing deleted, nothing hidden. Her post was on her profile, stamped 23:00:00.

23:00:00  fanout  post 30117  @oriane  1,890,000 timelines  queued
23:00:15  fanout  post 30118  @bex           180 timelines  done
23:00:32  fanout  post 30119  @tavish        150 timelines  done
23:00:53  fanout  post 30120  @sabeth        230 timelines  done
23:01:41  fanout  post 30121  @noemi         120 timelines  done
23:45:01  fanout  post 30117  @oriane  1,890,000 timelines  done

Kayode says nothing broke. Her post went down her follower list at 700 copies a second, and 1,890,000 copies take 2,700 seconds: 45 minutes. The four replies, 680 copies between them, took their turns along the way, which is why her last copy landed at 23:45:01, and why each reply was in its followers' timelines a second after it was posted. Most of the people who follow her friends follow her too.
For three quarters of an hour, the city read the answers before the question.

blocks.label: fanout_friday_2300.png

diagram.aria: Friday from 23:00:00 to 23:46:00. Oriane's copies are written from 23:00:00 to 23:45:01. The four replies are each copied within a second, at 23:00:15, 23:00:32, 23:00:53 and 23:01:41. Follower number 699,300 has replies from 23:00:53 and her post from 23:16:40. Follower number 1,587,600 has replies from 23:00:15 and her post from 23:37:49. The last follower in her list has replies from 23:00:15 and her post from 23:45:01.

blocks.caption: Kayode's fan-out log for Friday, redrawn. Her 1,890,000 copies ran from 23:00:00 to 23:45:01, while each reply was copied within a second. Follower #699,300 had replies from 23:00:53 and her post at 23:16:40; #1,587,600 had replies from 23:00:15 and her post at 23:37:49; the last follower in her list waited until 23:45:01.

blocks.text: Oriane will announce the wedding date soon, at night again. Kayode has four changes on the board. Which one do we make?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: A few words first. Copying each post into every follower's stored timeline when it's written is called fan-out on write, or push: reading a timeline is cheap, and a post costs one copy per follower. The other way round is fan-out on read, or pull: keep each account's posts once, and build a timeline at read time, when someone opens it, by gathering the newest posts of every account they follow. Now the evidence. Where in Oriane's follower list were the people who sent screenshots? How many accounts does a reader follow, how often are timelines opened at 23:00, and how much can the place that keeps everyone's own posts answer? And what were your seven workers doing at 03:00?

replies.author: u/whisperwall_nerys
replies.text: Kayode looked the screenshots up: nearly all came from the later part of her list. Paquita, who wrote in at 23:20, is number 1,587,600. A reader follows 180 accounts. At 23:00 we serve about 12,000 timeline reads a second. The posts store, which keeps each account's own posts once, answers at most 500,000 list reads a second; a list read fetches one account's newest posts. Besides Oriane, a typical reader follows 3 accounts with over 100,000 followers and 21 with over 10,000. The timeline cache, where the stored timelines live, takes at most 2,800 writes a second. At 03:00 the workers were idle.

comments.author: u/add_workers_dacre
comments.text: It's a capacity problem; add workers. Seven workers for a city of two million is a toy setup. Quadruple them: 28 workers is 2,800 copies a second, and her post is everywhere in about 11 minutes instead of 45. Nobody screenshots an 11-minute gap at 23:00 on a Friday. If that's still too slow, give the big accounts a priority lane, so their posts jump the queue and get copied before anything else. Workers are cheap. Rebuilding how your whole feed works is not.

comments.author: u/stellmarsh_paquita
comments.text: I was one of the screenshots. Bex's SHE SAID YES at 23:00, Sabeth's congratulations a few seconds before 23:01, Noemi's after that, and nothing to say who they were talking about. I asked three people in my building. Oriane's own post turned up at 23:37. I'd spent half an hour sure somebody I knew was getting married in secret.

reply.prompt: Oriane will post the wedding date soon, at night again. Which change should Kayode make before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Add more fan-out workers, so a post from a huge account reaches all its followers in minutes.
options.verdict: A shorter gap, the same shape
options.part2: Kayode went to 28 workers and replayed Friday in the lab. Her last copy landed at 23:11:16 instead of 23:45:01. The replies still landed a second after they were posted, so 533 of them still reached a timeline before her post did, down from 563. He tried 40 workers: 23:11:16 again, to the second. The timeline cache takes at most 2,800 writes a second, and 28 workers already fill it. In May Oriane posted the wedding date at 22:00. Her friends answered within two minutes, as before, and for about eleven minutes the tip inbox filled with screenshots of a date with no wedding attached. At 03:00 there were 28 workers with nothing to do.
options.senior: More workers shrink the gap but keep its shape: a huge account's post still costs one copy per follower, while a small account's reply costs a few hundred and overtakes it. And workers stop helping at whatever the timeline cache can take. The cost of a post has to stop growing with the poster's follower count.

options.text: Stop copying: build each timeline when it is opened, from the posts of every account it follows.
options.part2: Kayode built it on a test copy. Nothing was copied: her post was one write, and every follower had it at 23:00:00, before any reply. Then he looked at the reads. Each timeline read now gathered the newest posts of 180 accounts and merged them, so 12,000 reads a second at 23:00 meant 2,160,000 list reads a second, 4.32 times what the posts store answers. At 6,000 reads, a quiet hour, it was still 1,080,000, 2.16 times. We turned it on for one Tuesday evening anyway. Timelines spun, then came back empty, and the tip inbox filled with a different screenshot: an app with nothing in it.
options.senior: Pull is a real design and makes posting cheap: one write per post, whoever posts. But it moves the work to every read, and reads usually far outnumber posts; the cost is timeline reads a second times accounts followed. It fits where reads are rare or follow lists are short. For a busy home timeline, most of that work is better done once, at write time, for the accounts where it's cheap.

options.text: Push posts from ordinary accounts; pull the few huge accounts at read time, and merge the two.
options.part2: Kayode drew the line at 100,000 followers. Posts from accounts under it are copied as before. Oriane's posts, and those of every other account over the line, are stored once and read when a timeline is opened, then merged into the cached timeline by time. Friday replayed: her post was one write, every follower had it at 23:00:00, each reply arrived a second after it was posted, and none came before her post. Each timeline read is the cached timeline plus 4 list reads: 48,000 a second at 23:00, about a tenth of what the posts store answers. He tried 10,000 too: 22 list reads a timeline, 264,000 a second, and 528,000 at the 24,000 reads of a busy evening, over the limit. He kept 100,000. In May Oriane posted the wedding date at 22:00. The first screenshot in the tip inbox had her post at the top, and the replies under it.
options.senior: Push for the many accounts whose posts are cheap to copy, and pull the few whose follower counts make copying slow, merging the two at read time by post time. Most posts still cost a few hundred copies, most reads stay one cached timeline plus a few lists, and no post's cost grows with a celebrity's followers. Choose the threshold from your numbers: too low and reads drift towards pull's cost, too high and big posts lag again.

options.text: Give huge accounts a priority lane, so their posts are copied before any other post in the queue.
options.verdict: No reply first, because no reply at all
options.part2: Kayode let big posts jump the fan-out queue and replayed Friday. Her last copy landed at 23:45:00, one second sooner. No reply reached a timeline before her post, because no reply reached a timeline at all: all four were held until 23:45:01, and Bex's waited 44 minutes 47 seconds. In the lab, any post behind hers waits the same way. In May Oriane posted the wedding date at 22:00, and for three quarters of an hour nobody else in Stellmarsh could post anything that reached a timeline. The first screenshot in the tip inbox was of a timeline that had shown nothing new for forty minutes.
options.senior: A priority lane changes who waits, not how much work there is. 1,890,000 copies at 700 a second still take 45 minutes, and everything behind them waits too: the replies, and every other account's posts. It hides the eerie symptom by starving everyone else.

sim.title: Replay Friday night on Whisperwall
sim.lede: You're Nerys, replaying Friday from 23:00:00 to 23:50:00. Oriane posts at 23:00:00 to 1,890,000 followers. Her friends reply: Bex at 23:00:14 (180 followers, 150 of whom follow Oriane), Tavish at 23:00:31 (150, 120), Sabeth at 23:00:52 (230, 200) and Noemi at 23:01:40 (120, 100); the followers they share with her are spread evenly through her follower list. The lab counts only these five posts. Each fan-out worker copies 100 timelines a second, and the timeline cache takes at most 2,800 writes a second. Her post is copied in follower-list order; the workers take turns between posts, so a reply is copied from the second after it is posted. A reader follows 180 accounts; besides Oriane, a typical reader follows 21 accounts over 10,000 followers, 3 over 100,000 and none over 1,000,000. The posts store answers at most 500,000 list reads a second. Pull builds each timeline from 180 list reads. The hybrid, which pushes most accounts and pulls the accounts over its follower threshold, reads the cached timeline plus one list read per such account. The six boxes at the bottom are six of her followers, numbered by their place in her list. The clock runs 60 times faster than real life. Click any box to see what it is.
sim.tryThis: Try this: press Skip to 23:50 as it is: her last copy at 23:45:01, and 563 replies seen before their post. Then add workers: 28, then 40. Try big posts first, and read how long Bex's reply waited. Try pull for everyone and read the posts store's load at each read rate. Last, the hybrid: try each threshold, then set her followers to 50,000.

explain.oneLine: Nothing was hidden. Whisperwall copies every post into each follower's timeline, so Oriane's one post was 1,890,000 copies, 45 minutes at 700 a second, while her friends' replies, under 250 copies each, were everywhere within a second. 563 times, a reply reached a timeline before the post it answered.

steps.title: Fan-out on write turns one post into one copy per follower.
steps.text: Push makes reading cheap: opening the app is one read of a timeline that's already built. The bill comes at write time, one copy per follower. For most accounts that's a few hundred copies. For Oriane it was 1,890,000, and at 7 workers of 100 a second that is 2,700 seconds: 45 minutes. This is the celebrity problem: a few accounts with huge follower counts make the write side slow and expensive for everyone.

steps.title: Small posts overtake big ones.
steps.text: Her friends' replies cost 180, 150, 230 and 120 copies, done in their first turn, so each was in its followers' timelines a second after it was posted. Her copies went down her list in order: follower #699,300 got her post at 23:16:40, #1,587,600 at 23:37:49, the last at 23:45:01. Every friend's follower who sat late in her list saw the answer first: 563 times across the four replies. Nothing was lost. Only the order was wrong.

steps.title: More workers and a priority lane only move the wait.
steps.text: 28 workers bring her last copy to 23:11:16, but the replies are still faster: 533 before their post. Past 28, the timeline cache's 2,800 writes a second is the ceiling. Letting her post go first gets her last copy to 23:45:00 and holds every reply, and every other post, until it's done: Bex's waited 44 min 47 s. Neither changes what a post costs, one copy per follower.

steps.title: Fan-out on read moves the bill to every read.
steps.text: Pull keeps each post once and builds a timeline when it's opened: one write for her post, and nothing out of order. But every read gathers the newest posts of 180 accounts and merges them: at 12,000 reads a second, 2,160,000 list reads a second, 4.32 times the posts store's limit. Timelines are read far more often than anyone posts, which is why pure pull is rare for a busy home timeline.

steps.title: The hybrid: push the many, pull the few, merge.
steps.text: Copy posts from accounts under a follower threshold, as now. Store the posts of the few accounts over it once, and read them when a timeline is opened, merging them into the cached timeline by time. At 100,000, her post is one write, a read is the cached timeline plus 4 list reads (48,000 a second), and no reply comes before its post. The timeline cache is still a cache: keep only each timeline's newest entries, and only for people who use the app, and rebuild the rest from the posts store when they return.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for the wedding date. Bex's reply, from an account under 100,000 followers, is copied by the fan-out workers into the timeline cache, one list per reader. Oriane's post, from an account over 100,000, is written once to the posts store. A timeline read takes the cached timeline and 4 list reads from the posts store and merges them by time, so her post comes first and the replies under it.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for the wedding date. Posts from accounts under 100,000 followers are still copied into the timeline cache. Oriane's post is written once to the posts store. Each timeline read merges the cached timeline with 4 list reads by time, so her post is at the top from 23:00:00 and the replies sit under it.

fix.title: The fix: push most accounts, pull the few huge ones, merge at read time
fix.text: Set a follower threshold, 100,000 here. Posts from accounts under it go on the fan-out queue and are copied into each follower's cached timeline, as now. Posts from accounts over it are written once to the posts store and not copied. When a timeline is opened, read the cached timeline, read the newest posts of each account over the threshold that the reader follows, and merge them by post time, keeping each post id once. Keep each cached timeline to its newest entries, and skip copying to readers who haven't opened the app in a long time; rebuild theirs from the posts store when they return. Watch the age of the oldest post on the fan-out queue, so a slow fan-out is seen before the screenshots arrive, and recheck the threshold as accounts grow.

limits: Reads cost more for people who follow many big accounts, and the threshold decides how many. At 10,000, the sim's typical read is the cached timeline plus 22 list reads: 264,000 a second, and 528,000 at 24,000 reads, over the posts store's limit. Pick it from your own numbers and revisit it as accounts grow.

The huge accounts' newest posts are now read on nearly every timeline read, which makes them hot keys (Hot Key). Keep each big account's recent posts in a cache close to the readers, or in several copies, so one account's list isn't asked thousands of times a second in one place.

An account that crosses the threshold changes path. Posts copied before the switch and posts read after it can both appear, or neither: merge by post id so a post shows once, and handle the switch on purpose, with a margin so an account doesn't flip back and forth, and a backfill when it drops back under.

head: Design
Good
Bad
rows: A read is 1 cached timeline. Small posts arrive in a second.
Her post: 1,890,000 copies, last at 23:45:01; 563 replies before their post.
533 replies still first; past 28 workers no faster (cache limit 2,800 a second); idle most of the night.
No reply before her post; last copy at 23:45:00.
Every reply held until 23:45:01; Bex's waited 44 min 47 s; every other post waits too.
1 write a post; everyone has her post at 23:00:00.
180 list reads a timeline: 2,160,000 a second, 4.32 x the posts store's limit.
1 write for her post; no reply first; a read is the cache + 4 lists, 48,000 a second.
A merge on every read; big accounts' lists run hot; accounts crossing the line need care.

explain.seniorTake: A feed is a choice of when to pay: at write time, once per follower, or at read time, once per account followed. Push wins for almost everyone, because timelines are read far more often than anyone posts and most accounts are small; pull wins for the few accounts whose follower counts make a post's copies take minutes. So do both: push below a threshold, pull above it, and merge at read time by post time and id. Then say the costs out loud: a merge on every read, hot keys on the big accounts, a threshold to tune, and accounts crossing it to handle. And treat the timeline cache as a cache: bounded per timeline, kept only for active readers, and rebuildable from the posts.

realWorld.title: Twitter, QCon San Francisco 2012: Timelines at Scale
realWorld.text: The talk's published summary says Raffi Krikorian explains the architecture used by Twitter to deal with thousands of events per sec: tweets, social graph mutations, and direct messages. The slides published with it set out the challenge as more than 150M world wide active users, more than 300K QPS for timelines, and that naïve timeline "materialization" can be slow.

realWorld.title: Fan-out into Redis lists
realWorld.text: In the slides, each tweet passes from a Write API to a Fanout service, which writes into a Timeline Cache made of Redis. The insert is keyed off "recipient", pipelined 4k "destinations" at a time, and replicated. The cache uses Redis's native list structure, with RPUSHX to only add to cached timelines, and each entry is a Tweet ID (8 bytes), a User ID (8 bytes) and Bits (4 bytes).

realWorld.title: O(n) write, O(1) read
realWorld.text: One slide sets the timeline cache, O(n) write and O(1) read, against the search index (Earlybird), O(1) write and O(n) read: the same push and pull choice this case is about.

realWorld.title: The celebrity problem, on a slide
realWorld.text: A slide titled the challenge (part #2) says fanout can be really slow! ...especially for high follower counts. The next ones list @ladygaga with 31 million followers, @katyperry and @justinbieber with 28 million, @barackobama with 23 million, and then: there are over 400 million tweets a day, and 4600 tweets a second.

realWorld.title: The hybrid, as a query
realWorld.text: A later slide expands @raffi's home timeline into home_timeline:raffi OR user_timeline:taylorswift13: the stored home timeline, merged at read time with one huge account's own timeline. That is the hybrid this case ends on.

realWorld.title: Stream, 2026: pure push or pure pull rarely makes sense
realWorld.text: In a February 2026 post on scalable activity feeds, Stream's Raymond F writes that a celebrity with 10 million followers posting once means 10 million writes, and that pure push or pure pull rarely makes sense at scale. Its example rules: push to all followers for normal users (< 10K followers), store once and pull on read for high-fanout accounts (celebrities, brands), and skip push for inactive followers (not logged in for 30+ days), pulling on read if they return. The numbers are one vendor's rules of thumb, not a standard.

asked: How do you handle accounts with millions of followers?
interview.answer: Start with the two ways to build a timeline. Push, or fan-out on write: when someone posts, copy the post id into each follower's cached timeline, so a read is one lookup; the cost is one write per follower. Pull, or fan-out on read: store each post once and gather the newest posts of everyone the reader follows when the timeline is opened; the cost is one list read per account followed, on every read. Then do the arithmetic. Timelines are read far more often than anyone posts, so push wins for most accounts. But an account with millions of followers makes push slow: 1,890,000 copies at 700 a second is 45 minutes, and small accounts' replies overtake the post they answer. So use a hybrid: push for accounts under a follower threshold, pull the few over it at read time, and merge by time, keeping each post id once. Choose the threshold from read rate times big accounts followed against what the posts store can serve. Cap each cached timeline to its newest entries and skip copying to inactive users, rebuilding theirs when they return. Then the costs: a merge on every read, hot keys on the big accounts' lists, and accounts that cross the threshold need a margin and a backfill. More fan-out workers or a priority lane only move the wait.

Where readers send gossip tips and screenshots for Yolanda Fitzroy's Overheard column. Nerys sorts it at night.
Yolanda Fitzroy's gossip column on Whisperwall, written from readers' tips.
An account that follows another to see its posts in its own timeline. Not the replication follower of earlier cases.
The list of an account's followers, in a fixed order. Whisperwall's fan-out copies a post down it from the top.
What a reader sees on opening the app: the posts of the accounts they follow, newest first. Also called a home timeline or feed.
A timeline built in advance and kept ready, so opening the app is one read. Whisperwall keeps them in the timeline cache.
The in-memory store that holds every stored timeline, one list per reader. Whisperwall's takes at most 2,800 writes a second.
One reader's stored timeline in the timeline cache: a list of post ids, newest first.
The queue new posts wait on until the fan-out workers copy them to followers.
A worker that takes a post from the fan-out queue and copies it into followers' stored timelines. Each of Whisperwall's copies 100 a second.
One write of a post's id into one follower's stored timeline. A post to 1,890,000 followers is 1,890,000 copies.
Copying each post into every follower's stored timeline when it is posted. Reads are cheap; a post costs one copy per follower.
Keeping each post once and building a timeline when it is opened, from the newest posts of every account followed. Posts are cheap; every read does the work.
A few accounts with huge follower counts make fan-out on write slow and costly: each of their posts is millions of copies.
Push posts from accounts under a follower threshold, pull posts from the few accounts over it at read time, and merge the two.
The follower count above which an account's posts are pulled at read time instead of copied. 100,000 in the fix.
The moment a reader opens a timeline. Pull and the hybrid do their gathering then.
Combining the cached timeline with posts read from big accounts into one list, ordered by post time, each post once.
Where each account's own posts are kept once. Whisperwall's answers at most 500,000 list reads a second.
One fetch of one account's newest posts from the posts store.
One reader opening or refreshing their timeline. Whisperwall serves about 12,000 a second at 23:00.

terms.term: Work per timeline read (in the sim)
terms.def: What one timeline read costs: 1 cached timeline (push), 180 list reads (pull), or 1 cached timeline plus a list read per big account followed (hybrid).
Letting some posts jump the fan-out queue, so their copies are written before anything else.
To keep some work waiting indefinitely because other work always goes first.

terms.term: Replies seen before their post (in the sim)
terms.def: Followers of a friend, among the ones who also follow Oriane, whose timeline got that friend's reply before her post. 563 on Friday.
A morning radio or TV programme. Oriane hosts Stellmarsh's, which is why so many accounts follow her.
A unique number for each post. Timelines store ids, and a merge keeps each id once.
Copying an account's recent posts into followers' timelines after the fact, for example when it drops back under the threshold.
A gap between the counts that switch an account to pull and back to push, so one that hovers near the line doesn't flip back and forth.
An account that hasn't opened the app for a long time. Copying posts to its timeline is wasted work.
Dropping a cached timeline's oldest entries so it keeps only the newest few hundred.
Who follows whom: the accounts and the follow links between them.
Queries per second: how many requests a system answers each second.
Building a timeline and storing the result, so it's ready before anyone reads it.
A Redis value that is an ordered list, which can be added to at either end. Twitter kept each cached timeline as one.
A Redis command that adds to the end of a list only if the list already exists, so posts go only to timelines already in the cache.
Sending many commands to a server in one go without waiting for each answer, to cut round trips.
Twitter's search index service in the 2012 slides: each tweet is written once, and a search reads from many index parts.
Shorthand for how work grows: O(n) grows with n (here, followers or accounts followed), O(1) stays the same.
A list of recent actions by the people or things you follow, such as posts, likes or comments. A timeline is one.
A company that sells activity feeds and chat as a hosted service, and publishes engineering posts about them.
A company's private website for its own staff, often with news and announcements.
The SOC 2 availability point on capacity: monitoring and evaluating processing capacity against demand.

atWork: Look for a place where one person's message is copied to many people's feeds or inboxes. A common incident is a company intranet where a chief executive's announcement took about an hour to reach everyone: the intranet copied each announcement into every employee's feed, one write per employee, while a team lead's reply to it reached a few dozen colleagues in a second, and some staff read the replies first. Read-only access is enough. Find how your feed, inbox or notification list is built: copied when written, gathered when read, or both? For the account with the most followers, how many writes does one post cost, at what rate, and how long does that take? What does one read cost for a user who follows many accounts? Is there a threshold, and who chose it, from what numbers? Is each cached list capped, and is it kept for users who never log in? If your company is pursuing SOC 2 with availability in scope, criterion A1.1 asks, roughly, that processing capacity is monitored and evaluated against demand; a measured figure for your biggest account's fan-out time, and your feed reads' load against their limits, is that kind of evidence.

recall.prompt: Your city's football club app copies each post into every follower's stored timeline when it's posted. The club's own account has 600,000 followers; fans have a few hundred each. On match nights fans complain that their timelines fill with replies like 'What a goal!' up to 15 minutes before the club's goal post appears. The team wants to buy more fan-out workers. What is happening, and what do you recommend?

keyIdeas.idea: The club's post costs one write per follower, so it takes minutes to reach everyone, while a fan's reply costs a few hundred and overtakes it
More workers only shrink the delay; each post still costs a copy per follower, and the cache's write limit caps the speed
Use a hybrid: don't copy the club's posts; read them at read time and merge them into each fan's cached timeline

recall.model: The app does fan-out on write, so the club's post costs one write per follower: 600,000 copies, which take minutes at the fan-out's rate, written down the follower list in order. A fan's reply costs a few hundred copies and lands in a second, so fans late in the club's list get the replies first: small posts overtake the big one. That's the celebrity problem. More workers only shrink the delay: each post still costs a copy per follower, the timeline cache's write limit is a ceiling, and the replies stay faster. Use a hybrid instead: above a follower threshold, don't copy an account's posts. Store the club's posts once, read them at read time when a fan opens the timeline, and merge them with the cached timeline by time, so the goal post is there from the moment it's posted and the replies sit under it.

recall.prompt: Whisperwall's fan-out runs 7 workers, each copying 100 timelines a second. With nothing else posted, how long does one post to 1,890,000 followers take to reach its last follower?
recall.why: 7 x 100 = 700 copies a second, and 1,890,000 / 700 = 2,700 seconds: 45 minutes. On Friday the four replies' 680 copies took their turns along the way, so the last copy landed at 23:45:01. One worker alone would take 18,900 seconds, 5 hours 15 minutes; 4 and a half minutes would need 7,000 copies a second, more than the timeline cache's 2,800.

recall.prompt: Your photo app pushes every post into each follower's cached timeline, and the timeline cache's memory keeps growing. Each timeline keeps every entry ever copied into it, whole posts with their captions, and about 40 percent of accounts haven't opened the app in months. What would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: Cap each cached timeline to its newest few hundred entries and read older ones from the posts store on scroll
Stop copying to inactive accounts, and rebuild their timeline when they come back
Store post ids in the timeline, not whole posts, and fetch the posts when reading

recall.model: Treat the timeline cache as a cache, not the record. Keep only each timeline's newest few hundred entries and trim the rest; someone scrolling further back gets older posts from the posts store. Stop copying to inactive accounts: copy only to timelines that are already in the cache (Twitter's slides use RPUSHX for this), and rebuild a returning user's timeline from the posts of the accounts they follow when they come back. And store post ids in each timeline, not whole posts with captions; at read time, fetch the posts for the ids on screen. Each change cuts memory without slowing the reads that matter.

recall.prompt: In the sim, Kayode lets Oriane's post jump the fan-out queue, with 7 workers. What happens on Friday's replay?
options: Her last copy lands at 23:11:16, and 533 replies still come first.
Her last copy lands at 23:45:00, and every reply waits until 23:45:01.
Every follower has her post at 23:00:00, and the posts store is 4.32 times over its limit.
Her post is one write, and each timeline read is the cached timeline plus 4 list reads.
recall.why: A priority lane doesn't change the work: 1,890,000 copies at 700 a second still take 2,700 seconds, so her last copy lands at 23:45:00, one second sooner than as built. No reply comes before her post because every reply waits behind it until 23:45:01; Bex's waited 44 min 47 s, and every other post in the queue would wait the same way. 23:11:16 is 28 workers, 4.32 times is pull for everyone, and 4 list reads is the hybrid.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 4 months later. The hybrid has run since spring with the line at 100,000 followers, and the wedding date reached everyone at once. Then in August a video of Tavish's dog went round the city. His account went from 150 followers to 104,000 over a weekend and crossed the line on Sunday afternoon; from then on his posts were read at read time instead of copied. On Monday the inbox had screenshots of his Saturday post shown twice in the same timeline. On Thursday he fell back to 98,000 followers, and his posts from Sunday to Thursday vanished from his followers' timelines, though they're still on his profile.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did Tavish's posts show twice and then vanish, and what should change?

keyIdeas.idea: His Saturday post was copied before the switch and also read after it; the merge must keep each post id once
Posts he made while over the line were never copied, so dropping back under hides them; backfill them, or keep reading them
Don't let an account flip on every small change: use a margin, two thresholds, or a minimum time before switching back

coldCase.model: Both problems come from the switch between paths. His Saturday post had already been copied into his followers' cached timelines; after Sunday the merge also read it from the posts store, and nothing removed the repeat. Make the merge keep each post id once. Then the reverse: posts he made while over the line were never copied, so when he dropped back under, the timelines had no copy and the merge stopped reading his posts. When an account goes back to push, backfill its recent posts into its followers' timelines, or keep reading its posts for a while. And add a margin, for example switch to pull above 100,000 and back to push only below 80,000, with a minimum time between switches, so an account hovering near the line doesn't flip back and forth.

sources.title: Raffi Krikorian, Timelines at Scale, QCon San Francisco 2012, dated 3 April 2013 on the InfoQ page (summary: the architecture used by Twitter to deal with thousands of events per sec; slides published with the talk: over 150M active users and 300K QPS for timelines, Fanout into a Redis Timeline Cache, keyed off recipient, pipelined 4k destinations at a time, RPUSHX to only add to cached timelines, O(n) write and O(1) read, fanout can be really slow for high follower counts, home_timeline OR user_timeline)

Raymond F, How Do I Architect a Scalable Activity Feed System That Won't Crash Under Load?, Stream blog, 11 February 2026 (a celebrity with 10 million followers posting once means 10 million writes; pure push or pure pull rarely makes sense at scale; push for normal users, store once and pull on read for high-fanout accounts, skip push for inactive followers)
